subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 11 periods = 440 minutes
Total: 11 periods · 7h 20min

periods.activity_title: First Encounter: Reading the Story Aloud

time_bands.activity: Teacher invites students to share what they know about parrots — whether parrots can be clever, what it might feel like to live in a cage. Brief whole-class oral sharing sets a purpose for reading.

Teacher reads the narrative aloud from Textbook pp. 41–52, pausing at key moments — the parrot's request for freedom, the merchant's journey, and the parrot's dramatic fall — to model expressive reading and let the imagery settle.
Students follow along in their textbooks as the teacher re-reads the final episode (the parrot feigning death and escaping) with deliberate pacing, allowing them to track print and absorb the climax.
Teacher asks two or three spontaneous questions — 'What surprised you most?' and 'Was this ending what you expected?' — gathering first impressions without requiring a correct answer.

periods.teacher_notes: The narrative's turning point — the wild parrot's coded message — is subtle and may pass children by on first hearing; a brief pause and a gesture of surprise at that moment helps signal its importance. Allow children's first impressions to remain open-ended; precision comes in later encounters with the text.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think A (p.45): questions 1–3 — merchant's motive, parrot's appeal, coded message.

time_bands.activity: Teacher leads a shared re-reading of the opening pages of the story (pp. 41–44), with students reading alternate paragraphs aloud. Attention is on how the merchant and the parrot are described.

Class discusses Let us Think A questions 1, 2, and 3 from p. 45 — why the merchant kept the parrot in a golden cage, what made the parrot a favourite, and what message the parrot asked the merchant to carry. Teacher facilitates, inviting several students to respond to each question before moving on.
Students write their answers to the three discussed questions in their notebooks, using complete sentences. Teacher circulates and prompts where a child's reasoning is incomplete.
Two or three students share their written answers aloud. Teacher draws out the contrast between the merchant's wealth and the parrot's desire for freedom as the story's central tension.

periods.teacher_notes: Having listened to the full story read aloud, students are now ready to look closely at the text's early sections. Children often conflate 'favourite' with 'well-treated' — question 2 is a good place to tease apart those ideas by returning to what the story actually says about the parrot's gifts.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think A (p.45): questions 4–5 — the parrots' reaction and escape method.

time_bands.activity: Teacher guides students to re-read the episode of the merchant's jungle visit and his return home (pp. 45–49) silently, looking specifically for what happened when the message was delivered to the wild parrots.

Class works through Let us Think A questions 4 and 5 from p. 45 — what happened after the merchant delivered the message, and how the parrot finally escaped. Students discuss in pairs first, then share with the class.
Students write their answers to questions 4 and 5 in notebooks. Teacher guides those who are unsure back to the relevant passage, encouraging them to find textual evidence rather than guess.

Teacher consolidates by retelling the escape sequence in her own words, confirming students' answers and highlighting the narrative's key idea: the caged parrot's wit was the real source of its freedom.

periods.teacher_notes: The coded-message episode is the heart of the story's theme — wit over strength. Students sometimes say the wild parrot 'told' the caged one what to do, missing the cleverness of communicating through action; gently redirect them to what they read rather than what they assumed. Questions 4 and 5 anchor the story's resolution, so full written answers matter here.

periods.activity_title: Think, Discuss, and Listen: Freedom and Intelligence

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think B (p.45): discuss freedom, intelligence vs. strength, and which parrot is truly wise.
Let us Listen (p.48): teacher reads bird sanctuaries paragraph; students answer oral questions.

time_bands.activity: Class discusses Let us Think B questions from p. 45 — how students would respond to the parrot's request if they were the merchant, whether intelligence can be more useful than strength, and which parrot they consider truly wise. Teacher draws out multiple viewpoints without declaring one correct.
Teacher reads the listening paragraph about bird sanctuaries (p. 48) aloud clearly, at a measured pace. Students listen with books closed, attending to key facts.

Teacher reads the paragraph a second and third time, then asks oral factual questions — how many sanctuaries in India, which is oldest, which is largest. Students respond by raising hands; teacher confirms or gently corrects.

Brief whole-class reflection: teacher asks students to connect the listening content to the story — why might the parrot in the story have longed to join wild birds rather than remain caged? Students share thoughts freely.

periods.teacher_notes: The discussion questions in Let us Think B invite genuine divergence of opinion — the question of which parrot is 'wise' has no single answer, and validating different, well-reasoned responses models real intellectual discussion. The listening paragraph introduces factual content about Indian bird sanctuaries; accept any reasonable recall of numbers and names rather than demanding exact wording.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Speak A (p.48): listen-and-repeat 'ai' vs. 'oi' sound pairs.
Let us Speak B (p.49): picture-prompted sharing — caged or free bird, and why.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads each word pair from Let us Speak A (p. 48) — tail/toil, bail/boil, ail/oil, fail/foil, cane/coin, sail/soil — with clear articulation, and students repeat each pair chorally. Teacher then calls individual rows to say selected pairs, listening for accurate vowel distinction.

Students look at the two pictures on Textbook p. 49 — a parrot in a cage and a parrot flying free. Teacher gives a moment of quiet thinking time before inviting students to decide which bird they would want to be and why.

Students share their views one by one in Let us Speak B format from p. 49. Teacher encourages full sentences and probes with 'What would you enjoy most?' or 'What would you miss?' to extend responses beyond a single word.
Teacher briefly notices the range of responses — some preferring safety, some preferring freedom — and ties this back to the story's own central question about what makes a good life for the parrot.

periods.teacher_notes: The 'ai' and 'oi' distinction is easily blurred at speed; model each pair slowly first, then at natural speed, so students hear both registers. The picture-speaking task connects personal opinion to the story's theme — accept any view that is coherently expressed, since the goal is sustained oral expression, not a particular opinion.

periods.activity_title: Phrasal Verbs in Context: Let us Learn A

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn A (p.46): fill blanks with phrasal verbs to complete the winter-morning paragraph.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes the seven phrases from the word bank on the board — stand upright, all over, look after, stepped out, went away, came across, about to — and reads each one aloud. Class discusses what each phrase means in ordinary speech before opening the textbook.

Teacher reads the paragraph from Let us Learn A (p. 46) aloud with blanks voiced as pauses. Students predict which phrase fits each gap, raising hands to suggest. Teacher confirms or revisits meaning where predictions go astray.

Students complete the paragraph in their notebooks individually, filling all seven blanks. Teacher moves through the room, noting common errors — particularly confusion between 'came across' and 'went away' — and addresses them with the class.

Whole-class check: teacher reads the completed paragraph sentence by sentence, students call out their chosen phrase. Any discrepancies are discussed with reference to the meaning of the phrase in context.

periods.teacher_notes: Children at this stage often select phrases based on word familiarity rather than contextual fit; the phrase 'about to' is particularly prone to misplacement. Drawing attention to the sentence that follows each blank — what logically happens next — helps students check their choices against the paragraph's story logic.

periods.activity_title: Collective Nouns: Let us Learn B

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn B (p.46): complete sentences with collective nouns from the word bank.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces collective nouns using the example already given in the textbook — 'a flight of parrots' — connecting it directly to the story's jungle scene. Students suggest other groups they know before the word bank is revealed.

Teacher displays the word bank (pack, bouquet, army, flock, bunch, flight, swarm) and plays a quick oral matching game: teacher names an animal or object group, students call out the collective noun. This runs orally before students write.

Students complete sentences 2–7 from Let us Learn B (p. 46) in their notebooks. Teacher circulates, paying particular attention to the distinction between 'flock' (birds or sheep) and 'pack' (wolves), which students frequently conflate.

Students swap books with a partner and check each other's answers against the word bank. Teacher reads the correct answers aloud and students self-correct, noting which collective noun surprised them most.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read about a flock of parrots in the narrative, students have an authentic memory-hook for that particular collective noun — use it to anchor the whole group. 'Army of ants' is typically the most memorable for children; treat it as the springboard for the others rather than leaving all seven equally unanchored.

periods.activity_title: Present Perfect Tense: Let us Learn C

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn C (pp.47–48): present perfect tense — form and sentence completion.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the two example sentences from Let us Learn C (p. 47) — 'I have come from Jalandhar' and 'Rita has read all the poems' — and explains the rule: subject + has/have + past participle + object. Students echo the rule and identify has/have in each example.

Teacher works through sentence (a) with the whole class as a model — 'I have visited Delhi many times' — and then invites students to attempt (b) and (c) aloud before writing. Common verb forms (visited, drawn, bought) are discussed to ensure students know past participles.

Students complete sentences (a)–(e) from p. 47–48 individually in their notebooks, applying has or have as appropriate. Teacher circulates, noting where children use simple past instead of present perfect.

Answers are reviewed together: teacher calls on different students for each sentence and writes the correct form on the board, underlining has/have + past participle so the pattern is visually reinforced.

periods.teacher_notes: The most common error is substituting simple past ('she drew') for present perfect ('she has drawn') — this is worth addressing explicitly when reviewing sentence (b). Tying the tense to the story — 'The merchant has returned from his journey' — helps students feel the present relevance that defines this tense.

periods.activity_title: Continuing the Parrot's Story: Let us Write

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write (p.52): imagine and write what happens after the parrot escapes the golden cage.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the story continuation prompt aloud from Textbook p. 52 — 'After escaping from the golden cage, the parrot decided to fly away…' — and invites students to think silently about where the parrot might go and what it might feel. Two or three students share ideas aloud to seed the class imagination.

Teacher models planning on the board: a simple three-part plan — where the parrot flew, what it found there, how it felt at the end. Students copy this frame into their notebooks and jot their own ideas in each box before drafting.

Students draft their continuation using the prompt as their opening sentence. Teacher circulates, prompting students who are stuck with questions such as 'Does the parrot find its friends?' and 'What does freedom feel like for it?'

Students re-read their drafts quietly and make one or two revisions — checking for sense, adding a detail they left out, or improving an ending. Teacher moves through the room offering brief formative feedback.
Two students share their continuations with the class. Teacher offers warm, specific praise for elements that ring true to the story's spirit — wit, longing for freedom, or reunion with wild birds.

periods.teacher_notes: Children may end their stories very quickly — 'the parrot flew home and was happy' — without the narrative arc the task invites. The three-part planning frame helps them think past the first moment of escape to what happens next and what that means for the parrot. Full drafting AND a brief revision round fit comfortably within a single sitting.

periods.activity_title: Bird Feeders and Bird Facts: Let us Do and Let us Explore

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Do (p.50): identify materials in six feeder pictures; begin planning a feeder design.
Let us Explore (p.52): choose two birds from the ten illustrated and share interesting facts orally.

homework.task_brief: Let us Do (pp.50–51): make a bird feeder from your chosen material at home, fill it with seeds or millets, and place it outside with a family member's help.

time_bands.activity: Students open Textbook pp. 50–51 and examine the six photographs of bird feeders. Teacher guides a quick oral identification round — 'What is this one made from?' — working through plastic bottle, coconut shell, bamboo log, ice-cream stick box, clay bowl, and juice carton in turn.

Students choose the material they would use to make their own feeder and sketch a simple design in their notebooks, labelling parts. Teacher asks a few students to explain their choices to the class before describing the homework task — making the feeder at home and placing it outside.

Students turn to Textbook p. 52 and look at the ten labelled bird illustrations. Each student selects two birds and shares one or two interesting facts — real or from prior knowledge — with a partner. Teacher invites four or five pairs to share with the class, adding a fact of her own where knowledge is thin.

Teacher wraps up by connecting the bird-feeder and bird-exploration activities to the story's theme — when humans care for birds rather than caging them, birds flourish. Students are reminded to complete the feeder at home.

periods.teacher_notes: The feeder identification is purely oral and observation-based — no written answers are needed. The bird-facts sharing is deliberately open: students may draw on personal knowledge, family stories, or guesses, and the goal is enthusiastic engagement rather than accuracy. Setting the feeder task as homework keeps the making act itself outside class while the planning and discussion happen here.

periods.activity_title: Whole-Chapter Synthesis: Wit, Words, and Wings

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens with a quick oral quiz connecting all the chapter's language work: 'Give me a collective noun for wolves — now use it in a present perfect sentence.' Two or three rounds warm up vocabulary and grammar together.

Students retell the story of the wise parrot in pairs — one partner covers the first half (the merchant's journey and the jungle visit), the other covers the second half (the parrot's ruse and escape). Pairs then join into groups of four and compare their retellings, noticing any gaps.

Whole class composes a four-sentence summary of the story together: teacher scribes each sentence on the board as students contribute it, then reads the finished summary aloud. Students copy it into their notebooks as a model of concise summarising.

Teacher poses the chapter's central question — 'Was it wrong of the parrot to trick the merchant?' — and students debate briefly in two teams. This draws on the freedom theme from the oracy discussions and the story's moral, connecting reading, oracy, and beyond-text thinking.

Students write two sentences in response to the debate question, using a present perfect sentence as one of them — 'The parrot has proven that…' — to consolidate the grammar concept within their own thinking. Teacher reads two or three aloud to close the chapter.

periods.teacher_notes: This synthesis draws together the story's moral, the collective nouns and present perfect tense from the language work, and the freedom theme explored through speaking and the bird-feeder project. Students who find the debate difficult can be invited to say simply which parrot — caged or wild — they would rather be, a question already familiar from the speaking activity.

items.source_context: Merchant's motives for caging the parrot, coded message between parrots, escape through feigned death.
items.item_stem: Why did the wild parrot fall from the tree like a stone when the merchant delivered the caged parrot's message?

options.label: A
options.text: It had been injured by another animal and collapsed by chance.

options.label: B
options.text: It was angry with the merchant and tried to frighten him.

options.label: C
options.text: It was demonstrating to the merchant's parrot how to feign death in order to escape.

options.label: D
options.text: It was startled by a loud noise in the jungle.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Student may be guessing rather than tracing the plot's cause and effect.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student has read the fall literally and missed its coded, deliberate nature.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student has attributed motive to the wild parrot without following the story's logic.

items.source_lo: Student infers character motivation and traces plot causation using a narrative text as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Merchant's motives for caging the parrot, coded message between parrots, escape through feigned death.
items.item_stem: The merchant's parrot was described as talkative and entertaining. How did these very qualities both help it survive in the cage and ultimately help it win its freedom? Give reasons from the story in two or three sentences.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The parrot's entertaining nature — its stories and songs — made the merchant fond of it, which is why he kept it in a golden cage and valued it enough to deliver its message. That same trust in the parrot, combined with the parrot's quick wit in understanding the wild parrot's coded signal, allowed it to enact the plan of feigning death and win its freedom.

items.item_stem:
Your teacher will read the following passage aloud twice. Listen carefully, then answer the questions below.

Paragraph (teacher reads from Textbook p. 48): the bird sanctuaries passage about endangered birds, the more-than-70 sanctuaries in India, the Vedanthangal Sanctuary in Tamil Nadu as the oldest, and the Bharatpur Sanctuary in Rajasthan as the largest.

1. How many bird sanctuaries are there in India?
2. Which is the oldest bird sanctuary in India, and in which state is it located?

options.text: Bird sanctuaries are built to protect endangered birds and their species.
The Bharatpur Bird Sanctuary in Tamil Nadu is the oldest in India.
There are more than 70 bird sanctuaries in India.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Statement 1 is true. Statement 2 is false — the Bharatpur Sanctuary is in Rajasthan and is the largest, not the oldest; the Vedanthangal Sanctuary in Tamil Nadu is the oldest. Statement 3 is true.

items.item_stem: Look at the two pictures on Textbook page 49 — a parrot inside a cage and a parrot flying freely. Imagine you are one of these parrots. Tell the class which one you are, describe what your day feels like, and say whether you are happy with your life. Speak for about four to five sentences.

expected_elements: Names the chosen bird (caged or free).
Describes at least one feeling or daily experience.
States clearly whether the bird is happy and gives a reason.

items.item_stem:
Read the sentence below and choose the ending that best continues the parrot's story after it flies away from the merchant's windowsill.

After leaving the golden cage, the parrot flew towards the jungle because ___.

options.label: A
options.text: it had forgotten how to sing and hoped to practise in the trees.

options.label: B
options.text: it wanted to find the wild parrot who had sent it the coded message.

options.label: C
options.text: it was afraid of the open sky and preferred hiding in the forest.

options.label: D
options.text: the merchant had told it to leave and never return.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student has not connected the parrot's escape to its relationship with the wild flock.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student has misread the merchant's reaction — he was distressed, not dismissive.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student has projected a new, contradictory character trait onto the parrot.

items.source_context: Parrot's life after escaping the golden cage — imagined continuation of the story's ending.
items.item_stem: The story ends the moment the parrot spreads its wings and flies away. Continue the story in four to six sentences: where does the parrot go, who does it meet, and how does it feel when it is finally free? Begin your writing with: 'After escaping from the golden cage, the parrot decided to fly away…'

expected_elements: Names a place or character the parrot reaches.
Describes the parrot's feeling of freedom clearly.
Gives the continuation a logical ending or resolution.
